subject: Immunology
vignette: A 39-year-old man with untreated HIV presents with 3 weeks of progressive exertional dyspnea and a dry, nonproductive cough. He has had no fever, chills, or hemoptysis. On examination he is tachycardic but not tachypneic at rest, and chest auscultation reveals clear lung fields. Chest radiograph shows bilateral diffuse perihilar ground-glass opacities. His CD4+ T-cell count is 95 cells/mm3 and his HIV-1 RNA is 310,000 copies/mL. His lactate dehydrogenase is elevated at 480 U/L. Induced sputum testing confirms the diagnosis.
question: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management, in addition to initiating antiretroviral therapy?

options.text: Begin trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole for Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia and add prednisone if the PaO2 is below 70 mmHg
Begin four-drug therapy with rifampin, isoniazid, pyrazinamide, and ethambutol
Begin high-dose fluconazole for presumed Candida pneumonia
Begin ganciclovir with intravitreal injections for cytomegalovirus pneumonitis
Withhold specific antimicrobial therapy until antiretroviral therapy produces immune reconstitution

explanation_correct: A subacute dry cough, dyspnea on exertion, bilateral perihilar ground-glass opacities, elevated LDH, and a CD4 count below 200 cells/mm3 are the classic picture of Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia, and the absence of fever, chills, and focal findings is typical. First-line treatment is high-dose trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole; adjunctive corticosteroids are added when the arterial PaO2 is below 70 mmHg or the alveolar-arterial gradient is at least 35 mmHg, because hypoxemia triggers a damaging inflammatory response to dying organisms. Prophylaxis becomes an ongoing consideration once the episode resolves and the CD4 count remains below 200.

explanation_incorrect.B: The RIPE regimen targets tuberculosis, which usually produces fever, purulent or blood-tinged sputum, and focal apical infiltrates or cavitation rather than diffuse perihilar ground-glass opacities and a normal auscultatory examination.
explanation_incorrect.C: Candida causes esophageal, oropharyngeal, and vulvovaginal disease in HIV, and primary Candida pneumonia is extremely rare; the radiographic pattern here is not suggestive of it.
explanation_incorrect.D: Cytomegalovirus pneumonia is far less common, typically appears at CD4 counts below 50 cells/mm3, and would more often be accompanied by concurrent CMV retinitis or colitis.
explanation_incorrect.E: Untreated Pneumocystis carries a high mortality, so specific antimicrobial therapy must begin immediately; antiretroviral therapy is started concurrently but is never a substitute for prompt treatment.

educationalObjective: Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia in a patient with a CD4 count below 200 cells/mm3 is treated with trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, with corticosteroids added when PaO2 is under 70 mmHg.

subject: Immunology
vignette: A 44-year-old woman with a CD4+ T-cell count of 32 cells/mm3 and an undetectable HIV viral load after years of poor adherence presents with 3 weeks of progressive left-sided weakness, intermittent headache, and low-grade fever. Neurologic examination reveals right-sided pronator drift and a mild expressive aphasia. Contrast-enhanced brain MRI shows four ring-enhancing lesions with surrounding edema in the basal ganglia and gray-white junction. Serum IgG for Toxoplasma gondii is positive. Lumbar puncture is deferred because of mass effect and edema.
question: Which of the following is the most appropriate initial management?

options.text: Intravenous ganciclovir plus foscarnet
Empiric pyrimethamine plus sulfadiazine with leucovorin, and repeat imaging in 2 weeks
Immediate brain biopsy with excision of all lesions
High-dose fluconazole monotherapy
Liposomal amphotericin B plus flucytosine induction

explanation_correct: Multiple ring-enhancing lesions in a patient with severe CD4 depletion and a positive Toxoplasma serology strongly suggest toxoplasmic encephalitis, which is the most common cause of focal brain lesions in AIDS. Standard practice is to start empiric pyrimethamine plus sulfadiazine with leucovorin and reassess with imaging in about 2 weeks; clinical and radiographic improvement confirms the diagnosis and avoids the morbidity of biopsy. Brain biopsy is reserved for failure to improve, for seronegative patients, or when lymphoma or another diagnosis remains likely.

explanation_incorrect.A: Ganciclovir plus foscarnet treats cytomegalovirus, which typically causes retinitis or colitis and only very rarely produces multifocal ring-enhancing lesions in the basal ganglia.
explanation_incorrect.C: Immediate biopsy and excision is not the initial step, because an empiric Toxoplasma trial avoids an invasive procedure in a patient with a classic presentation and positive serology.
explanation_incorrect.D: Fluconazole is used for cryptococcal meningitis, which usually presents with headache, meningismus, and basal meningeal enhancement rather than multifocal parenchymal ring-enhancing lesions.
explanation_incorrect.E: Amphotericin B plus flucytosine is the induction regimen for cryptococcal meningoencephalitis and would not treat toxoplasmic encephalitis, whose therapy is pyrimethamine-based.

educationalObjective: Multiple ring-enhancing basal ganglia lesions in a severely immunocompromised patient with positive Toxoplasma IgG are treated empirically with pyrimethamine, sulfadiazine, and leucovorin rather than immediate biopsy.

subject: Immunology
vignette: A 36-year-old man with newly diagnosed HIV has a CD4+ T-cell count of 60 cells/mm3. He is asymptomatic and his physical examination is normal. His antiretroviral regimen includes tenofovir disoproxil fumarate plus emtricitabine plus efavirenz. The clinic pharmacist reviews his medications and flags a specific agent as a component of many first-line regimens that also carries activity against hepatitis B virus and therefore must not be stopped abruptly in a coinfected patient.
question: Which of the following nucleoside/nucleotide reverse transcriptase inhibitors is also used as treatment for chronic hepatitis B and can precipitate a hepatitis flare if discontinued without coverage?

options.text: Zidovudine
Abacavir
Tenofovir disoproxil fumarate
Doravirine
Raltegravir

explanation_correct: Tenofovir disoproxil fumarate and tenofovir alafenamide are nucleotide reverse transcriptase inhibitors with dual activity against HIV and hepatitis B virus, so they are preferred in patients with HIV/HBV coinfection. Abrupt discontinuation of tenofovir/emtricitabine (or lamivudine) in a coinfected patient can cause a severe hepatitis flare with transaminase elevation, which is why HBV-active therapy must be continued or transitioned carefully. Tenofovir is also a common cause of proximal tubulopathy and Fanconi-like syndrome through mitochondrial toxicity in proximal tubular cells, so renal function is monitored.

explanation_incorrect.A: Zidovudine is an HIV nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitor associated with bone marrow suppression and macrocytic anemia, and it has no meaningful role in treating chronic hepatitis B.
explanation_incorrect.B: Abacavir is a guanosine analogue effective against HIV only, and it is notable for the HLA-B*5701-associated hypersensitivity reaction and an increased risk of cardiovascular events.
explanation_incorrect.D: Doravirine is a non-nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitor that is active against HIV but has no activity against hepatitis B virus, so it does not produce the coinfection issue described.
explanation_incorrect.E: Raltegravir is an integrase strand transfer inhibitor and not a reverse transcriptase inhibitor at all, and it has no activity against hepatitis B virus.

educationalObjective: Tenofovir is a preferred dual-active agent for HIV/HBV coinfection, and stopping it abruptly in a coinfected patient can precipitate a hepatitis flare.

subject: Immunology
vignette: A 42-year-old woman is diagnosed with HIV after presenting with oral thrush. Her CD4+ T-cell count is 40 cells/mm3 and her viral load is 95,000 copies/mL. She is evaluated for latent tuberculosis with an interferon-gamma release assay, which is positive, and her chest radiograph is normal. She has never taken antiretroviral therapy and reports feeling well. The clinician identifies the major opportunistic pathogen most likely to cause disease when her CD4 count falls further, and considers prophylaxis.
question: Which of the following prophylactic agents is most appropriate for this patient at her current CD4 count, before antiretroviral therapy has raised it?

options.text: No prophylaxis is needed because her chest radiograph is normal
Azithromycin for Mycobacterium avium complex prophylaxis
Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole for Pneumocystis jirovecii prophylaxis
Isoniazid plus pyridoxine for treatment of latent tuberculosis
Fluconazole for Candida prophylaxis

explanation_correct: A positive interferon-gamma release assay with a normal chest radiograph indicates latent tuberculosis, and treatment of latent TB with isoniazid plus pyridoxine (to prevent peripheral neuropathy) is indicated, with weekly rifapentine plus isoniazid as an alternative. In HIV, treatment of latent TB should be completed regardless of CD4 count, and it is ideally completed before or with antiretroviral therapy; for most latent TB regimens, ART can be started shortly after initiation. Note that her CD4 count of 40 cells/mm3 also qualifies her for Pneumocystis and MAC prophylaxis, but the positive IGRA adds a distinct and more urgent indication.

explanation_incorrect.A: A normal chest radiograph excludes active pulmonary TB but does not exclude latent infection, and the positive interferon-gamma release assay specifically indicates latent disease requiring treatment.
explanation_incorrect.B: Azithromycin for MAC prophylaxis is indicated only when the CD4 count falls below 50 cells/mm3, and it is not the answer to the positive latent TB test the clinician has just identified.
explanation_incorrect.C: Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole is indeed indicated for PCP prophylaxis at a CD4 count below 200 cells/mm3, but the question asks about the indication created by the positive interferon-gamma release assay.
explanation_incorrect.E: Fluconazole prophylaxis is not routinely recommended because of cost, drug interactions, and the risk of selecting resistant Candida species, even in advanced HIV.

educationalObjective: A positive latent tuberculosis test in a patient with HIV warrants isoniazid plus pyridoxine therapy regardless of CD4 count, alongside CD4-based prophylaxis for PCP and eventually MAC.
